title: Getting around: ojek, taxi, train
goal: Move around an Indonesian city: order a motorbike taxi, direct a driver, buy a train ticket and understand the two verbs that carry all of it — *naik* and *turun*.
bekal: say how you are travelling with *naik*
give a driver instructions and stop him where you want
buy a ticket and ask how long the journey takes

notes: **Naik is "to ride, to go by, to board" — and also "to go up".** *Naik ojek*, *naik bus*, *naik pesawat*, *naik taksi*. Its partner *turun* is "to get off" and "to go down". Together they cover every journey in the country, and they never change form.

**Macet is a word you will use daily.** It means a traffic jam, and in Jakarta it is a permanent condition rather than an event. *Macet parah* is a bad one; *lumayan macet* is "fairly jammed"; *lancar* is the happy opposite — traffic flowing.

**Ojek is a motorbike taxi**, and app-based ones (Gojek, Grab) have transformed Indonesian cities. The driver will phone you to find you, which is why *Posisinya di mana?* — "where exactly are you?" — is worth memorising before you ever order one.

**Turun di… tells the driver where to stop.** You do not need a complicated sentence: *Turun di sini* ("stop here"), *Turun di depan* ("stop just ahead"), *Kiri, Mas!* ("pull over on the left!"). That last one is the standard shout on a public minibus.
**Lumayan** is a lovely little word meaning "quite, fairly, not bad". *Lumayan jauh* (fairly far), *lumayan enak* (quite tasty), and on its own, in answer to "how was it?", it means "not bad at all".

grammars.title: Naik — how you travel
body: The pattern is simply *naik* + the vehicle. No preposition, no article.

head: Indonesian
Word for word
English
rows: I'm going to Bandung by train.

after: The question is *Naik apa?* — "how are you getting there?", literally "ride what?". You will be asked this constantly, because in Indonesia the answer determines how long the journey will take far more than the distance does.
⚠️ *Naik* also keeps its literal meaning of going up: *naik tangga* (go up the stairs), *harga naik* (prices went up). Context always makes it obvious.

grammars.title: Talking to a driver
body: Ten sentences that cover almost every taxi and ojek ride you will ever take.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: Don't take that road, it's jammed.
Drop me in front of that building.

after: ⚠️ **Argo** is the taximeter. In an ordinary metered taxi, *pakai argo* is a reasonable request; if the driver refuses and offers a fixed price, that is your cue to agree a number **before** you set off, not after.
For app-based rides none of the bargaining applies — the price is fixed in the app, and the only sentences you need are the ones about where you are and where you want to be dropped.

blocks.text: Useful sentences at a counter: *Ada tiket ke Yogyakarta untuk besok?* (Is there a ticket to Yogyakarta for tomorrow?) — *Berangkat jam berapa?* (What time does it leave?) — *Sampai jam berapa?* (What time does it arrive?) — *Berapa lama perjalanannya?* (How long is the journey?).
💬 *Jam berapa berangkat?* and *Berangkat jam berapa?* are both correct. Indonesian is relaxed about where the time question sits, which is one more piece of freedom the language hands you.
Anto said *Kalau tidak macet, dua puluh menit*. *Kalau* introduces a condition, and Indonesian uses it far more loosely than English uses "if" — it also covers "when", "as for" and "in the case of".

head: Indonesian
Word for word
English
rows: If there's traffic, I'll be late.
if rain, we at home only
If it rains we'll stay home.
In that case, let's make it tomorrow.
Call me when you get there.

blocks.text: Notice the last line: *kalau* plus *sudah* is how Indonesian says "when" about something that has not happened yet. There is no future tense to worry about — the markers you learned in Unit 5 do all of it.
